subtype: Being cast as the lower role [Receiver]
passage: Honestly, Rafiq, the strangest part of the hotel traineeship wasn't the hours. It was the name. For six months I was 'trainee'. 'Trainee, towels.' 'Trainee, don't speak to guests unless asked.' We wore grey while staff wore blue. At first I kept a notebook of ideas, like moving the breakfast queue so it didn't block the lift. By month three I'd stopped writing in it. By month five, when a guest asked me something simple about check-out, I heard myself say, 'Sorry, I'm only the trainee, ask the desk.' I knew the answer. I'd just started believing I wasn't the kind of person who answers. And underneath, I was angry all the time at everyone in blue. The first time anyone there called me Jahnavi was my last day.

qa.q: What colour did the trainees wear?
qa.a: Trainees wore grey while staff wore blue.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say 'I'm only the trainee' despite knowing the answer?
qa.a: Jahnavi had come to feel small in the role, believing trainees are not the kind of people who answer.

qa.q: Which choice from the early months could Jahnavi return to?
qa.a: Jahnavi could pick up the notebook of ideas again, since it was the habit that kept Jahnavi's own voice alive before the role took over.

qa.q: How might a guest see a trainee who says 'ask the desk' to a simple question?
qa.a: The guest might think the trainee knows nothing, never guessing Jahnavi knew the answer and once planned a better breakfast queue.

grounding: A young adult tells how months cast as 'trainee' made them passive and resentful and led them to see themselves as the role.

passage:
I've roomed with Nandini since the first week of engineering college, so I watched it happen, though I can't say what was in her head. In August she arrived with a guitar and a hundred plans. Then came 'fresher period': seniors decided where first-years sat in the mess, what they wore on Mondays, when they could use the common room. Nandini followed all of it. By October she'd stopped taking the guitar out. When the class rep asked for fest volunteers, she said, 'Freshers don't get picked anyway.' Once, a senior she'd never met asked her to fetch his bag, and she just went, without a word, face flat. At night she started saying 'we're just juniors' about things that had nothing to do with seniors. I don't know exactly when she started believing it.
— Sunaina

qa.q: What did Nandini arrive with in August?
qa.a: She arrived with a guitar and a hundred plans.

qa.q: What does 'Freshers don't get picked anyway' suggest about how Nandini sees herself?
qa.a: It suggests Nandini now sees herself as the low role she is treated as, and gives up before trying.

qa.q: What small choice could help Nandini step outside the fresher role?
qa.a: Nandini could volunteer for the fest anyway, or take the guitar out again, doing one thing that belongs to her rather than to the role.

qa.q: Why can Sunaina describe the change but not be sure of its cause?
qa.a: Sunaina only sees the outside: the guitar left in its case, the flat face, the phrases; the moment Nandini began believing it stayed private.

grounding: A roommate observes a fresher growing passive and withdrawn under 'fresher period' rules until she speaks of herself as just a junior.

subtype: Being cast as the lower role [Receiver]
passage:
Day 1. Irfan, twenty-one, walked into the bank branch in a new shirt, carrying a list of questions. "Can I sit in on the loan desk?" The branch head laughed. "Trainees do photocopies." Pooja, the other trainee, rolled her eyes at him, friendly. "Welcome."
Week 4. The list of questions was gone. People called Irfan 'photocopy boy'. When a customer asked him about an account form, he pointed at the counter without looking up. At lunch Pooja said, "You used to talk more." He shrugged. "What's the point? We're furniture."
Week 8. Irfan snapped at the peon over a jammed machine, then sat staring at the queue, jaw tight. That night he wrote in his notebook: 'Maybe I'm just not a bank person.' He had forgotten the list of questions entirely.

qa.q: What did the branch head say trainees do?
qa.a: "Trainees do photocopies."

qa.q: What does Irfan's "We're furniture" reveal about how he now feels?
qa.a: It reveals Irfan feels worthless and resigned, starting to see himself as the role he has been given 😔

qa.q: What could Irfan choose after Pooja says "You used to talk more"?
qa.a: Irfan could dig out his list of questions and ask the branch head for one week at the loan desk, instead of shrugging.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Irfan changing?
qa.a: Pooja notices he talks less and cares enough to say so, remembering the eager trainee from Day 1.

grounding: Across three beats, a bank trainee treated as 'photocopy boy' grows passive and resentful and begins to see himself that way.

passage: Nandini, sit with your Farida Phuphi for a minute. You say you're only a trainee, so you keep quiet. I said the same thing once. At nineteen I joined a big tailoring house in Hyderabad as an apprentice. We were called 'the girls'. We swept, threaded needles, carried tea. The masters never asked what we thought. At first I carried a notebook of my own designs. By the fourth month I had stopped opening it. When a customer asked me about a sleeve, I said, 'Ask master-ji, I'm only the apprentice,' though I knew the answer better than he did. I went home angry every night, and I didn't even know at whom. The worst part was I started to believe I wasn't the kind of person who designs. It took a new master, years later, asking for my notebook, to remind me that the apprentice was a role, not me.

qa.q: What did Farida carry at first as an apprentice?
qa.a: She carried a notebook of her own designs.

qa.q: How did Farida come to think about herself as the months went by?
qa.a: She began to believe she was not the kind of person who designs, and felt angry every night without knowing at whom.

qa.q: What turning point helped Farida see herself differently?
qa.a: A new master asking for her notebook reminded her that being an apprentice was a role, not who she was.

qa.q: Why might Nandini hear this story differently from a lecture?
qa.a: Hearing that an aunt once said the same words might help Nandini see that staying quiet as a trainee is the role talking, not Nandini's true self.

grounding: An elder remembers how the apprentice role made her passive and resentful until she began to see herself as the role treated her.

subtype: Being cast as the lower role [Receiver]
passage: The monsoon had grounded half the flights, and the airport terminal was packed with angry passengers. Maria, twenty, six weeks into her ground-staff traineeship, stood in her grey trainee vest while the blue-vest staff ran the counters. Trainees were not to speak on the microphone or answer rebooking questions; for six weeks she had been told, "Trainee, move the trolleys," "Trainee, stay back." A mother with a baby asked her which counter handled the Kochi flight. Maria knew. She had studied the board all morning. But she heard herself say, "Sorry, I'm only a trainee, please ask the desk." The mother turned away, tired. Simran, the other trainee, looked at her. "You knew that." Maria shrugged, jaw tight. "What's the point? They don't want us to think." She pushed the next trolley harder than she needed to.

qa.q: What colour vest did the trainees wear?
qa.a: The trainees wore grey vests.

qa.q: Why did Maria say she was only a trainee even though she knew the answer?
qa.a: After six weeks of being treated as someone who only moves trolleys, she had started to see herself as the role, and she felt resentful about it.

qa.q: What could Maria do the next time she knows an answer?
qa.a: She could give the simple answer and point the passenger to the right counter, and ask her supervisor what trainees are allowed to help with.

qa.q: How might the mother with the baby have felt when Maria turned her away?
qa.a: The tired mother likely felt more frustrated and alone in the crowded terminal, since she did not get an answer the trainee could have given.

grounding: A trainee placed in a subordinate role becomes passive and resentful and starts to see herself as she is treated, even amid a crisis.
